script.title: Exploring Magnets: The Invisible Force
script.subtitle: Master the secrets of magnetic poles, attraction, and navigation.

steps.body: Check if the material is magnetic (iron, nickel, cobalt) or non-magnetic (plastic, wood).
Find the poles; magnetic strength is highest at the ends (North and South poles).
Bring two poles together: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

script.example: Question: If a bar magnet's North pole is brought near another North pole, what happens? Answer: They will repel each other because like poles exert a pushing force.
script.ctaBody: Try making your own magnet using the rubbing method!
script.videoPrompt: A 3D bar magnet floating in space, showing glowing North and South poles attracting iron filings.

topics.heading: Discovery of Magnets
topics.explain: Magnets were discovered by a shepherd named Magnes when his iron-tipped stick stuck to a rock. It is like a hidden superpower that certain rocks possess to pull metal objects.
bullets: Magnetic materials include iron, nickel, and cobalt.
topics.example: A magnet will pick up a steel nail but will not pick up an eraser.
topics.visual: A shepherd's staff sticking to a dark, rocky mountain side.

topics.heading: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials
topics.explain: Materials are divided into two groups based on their reaction to a magnet. Think of it like a VIP club where only certain metals are allowed to enter the magnetic field.
bullets: Testing is done by bringing a magnet close to the object.
topics.example: Testing a copper coin: It is non-magnetic and will not move.
topics.visual: A split screen showing a magnet pulling a nail vs. a magnet ignoring a pencil.

topics.heading: Poles of a Magnet
topics.explain: Every magnet has two ends called poles where the magnetic strength is strongest. It is like the two ends of a battery where the energy is most concentrated.
bullets: Poles always exist in pairs; you cannot have a single pole.
Magnetic strength is maximum at the poles.
topics.example: If you break a magnet in half, you get two smaller magnets, each with N and S poles.
topics.visual: A bar magnet glowing intensely at its two ends.

topics.heading: Finding Directions using a Magnet
topics.explain: A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest in the North-South direction. It acts like a natural compass that helps travelers find their way.
bullets: A suspended magnet aligns with Earth's magnetic field.
The North pole of the magnet points toward the Earth's North.
A magnetic compass uses a tiny magnetized needle for this.
topics.example: A sailor uses a compass to find North when lost at sea.
topics.visual: A compass needle spinning and then settling towards the North direction.

topics.heading: Attraction and Repulsion
topics.explain: Magnets interact based on their poles. Like poles push away, while different poles pull together. It is like two people either hugging or running away from each other.
bullets: Repulsion is the surest test for magnetism.
topics.example: Bringing the North pole of Magnet A to the North pole of Magnet B causes them to push apart.
topics.visual: Two bar magnets pushing away from each other with visible force lines.

script.misconception: Students often think a magnet only has one pole. Correction: Magnets ALWAYS have two poles (North and South); even if you break a magnet, new poles appear.
script.examTip: When describing attraction/repulsion, always use the terms 'Like poles repel' and 'Unlike poles attract' to get full marks.
